newsitem.title: USA: Any Fed tightening seen limited in scope - sources.
newsitem.headline: Any Fed tightening seen limited in scope - sources.

text.p: A bid by the Federal Reserve to stabilize the robust U.S. economic expansion is likely to involve only small interest rate adjustments, according to sources close to the central bank.

The current low inflation rate allows for a "recalibration" rather than a radical change to monetary policy because volatility in the inflation rate declines when inflation is already low, one source told Reuters.
Major swings in U.S. growth or inflation have triggered, in the past, protracted easing or tightening cycles.

Since it doubled the federal funds rate between February 1994 and February 1995, the Fed has moved on the overnight inter-bank lending rate only three times, lowering it to 5.25 percent in small, 25-basis-points increments.
The source said a small "recalibration, or adjustment," of monetary policy showed the U.S. economy was more stable, in large part due to the absence of inflation swings.

The Federal Open Market Committee next meets on March 25 to set the federal funds rate in an economic environment marked by rapid growth, tight labor markets, strong consumer spending and few price pressures.
The source stressed that the Fed is essentially concerned about incipient price pressures and the direction of underlying inflation, which has stopped heading lower.

"Looking at the asymmetric directive the Fed had in place for some time now, this indicates the Fed thinks inflation this year would be somewhat where it was last year or a little higher," the source also said, referring to the tightening bias introduced by the central bank last July.
"What justifies preemptive policy is that the cost in lowering inflation, once it picks up, would certainly be higher if you wait too long," the source noted.

"Policy must be preemptive, not reactive, to achieve price stability," the source said, explaining that an adjustment of the funds rate would mirror in scope the small easing moves made by the Fed between July 1995 and January 1996 to respond to a worrisome slowdown.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan described the last of those three moves -- which, with hindsight, appeared unnecessary -- as taking out "insurance."
In his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last month, Greenspan pointed out that one main difference between 1994 and 1997 was the level of the real, or inflation-adjusted, fed funds rate.

The real funds rate was close to zero and stimulative in 1994. In 1997, the real funds rate is at least 225 basis points, which Greenspan described as slightly restrictive and not particularly high by historic standards.
A second source close to the Fed said the major concern at the Fed is the high level of growth which is running, on average, clearly above trend for the fifth straight quarter.

"The (inflation) risks are on the upside given that the economy is still growing from already high levels of resource utilization," that source said. "Preemptive policy means the Fed does not have to slam on the brakes too hard."

The second source added that the economy seemed to have decelerated only slightly from its 3.9-percent pace recorded in the fourth quarter of 1996, despite the Fed's forecast for a slowdown in the second half of 1996.

Gross Domestic Product rose 3.2 percent on a fourth-quarter over fourth-quarter basis in 1996, well above the 2.0- to 2.5-percent range often cited by Fed officials as the long-term potential growth rate.
GDP growth in 1996 also represented a surge from 1.3 percent in 1995, and neared the 3.5-percent rate registered in 1994 when the Fed launched an aggressive preemptive tightening cycle.
